summary: This clipped Wikipedia article describes the Warsaw Pact, the Soviet-led Cold War collective defence treaty among the USSR and Central and Eastern European satellite states. It covers the Soviet motives for forming the pact (ideological control and geostrategic concerns about West German rearmament within NATO), its command structure dominated by the USSR, its military actions such as the 1956 Hungarian revolt and 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, and its dissolution in 1991.
one_line: Overview of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact alliance, its formation, Soviet domination, military interventions, and its dissolution in 1991.
key_facts: The Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 was the Pact's sole joint military action, and all members except Romania and Albania participated.
The Warsaw Pact was formally known as the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance and was signed in Warsaw, Poland.
The Warsaw Pact was created in reaction to the integration of West Germany into NATO in 1955, per the London and Paris Conferences of 1954.
The Brezhnev Doctrine explicitly stated the necessity of intervention if a country appeared to be violating core socialist ideas and Communist Party functions.

In 1956, after the Imre Nagy government declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, Soviet troops entered the country, removed the government, and crushed the nationwide revolt, leading to the death of an estimated 2,500 Hungarian citizens.

The Pact's Political Consultative Committee handled political matters, while the Combined Command of Pact Armed Forces controlled the assigned multi-national forces, with headquarters in Warsaw, Poland.
The Supreme Commander of the Unified Armed Forces of the Warsaw Treaty Organization was also a First Deputy Minister of Defense of the USSR.
The Pact was the military complement to the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CoMEcon), the regional economic organization for the socialist states of Central and Eastern Europe.
On 25 February 1991, the Pact was declared at an end at a meeting of defense and foreign ministers from the remaining member states meeting in Hungary.
On 1 July 1991, Czechoslovak President Václav Havel formally ended the Warsaw Treaty Organization in Prague, after 36 years of military alliance with the USSR.
The treaty was de facto disbanded in December 1989 during the violent revolution in Romania, which toppled the communist government, without military intervention from other member states.
NATO officials labeled the Warsaw Pact a 'cardboard castle' because of the rushed way in which it was conceived.

General Hastings Ismay said NATO "must grow until the whole free world gets under one umbrella" and opposed the 1954 Soviet request to join NATO, calling it "like an unrepentant burglar requesting to join the police force."
In July 1963 the Mongolian People's Republic asked to join the Warsaw Pact; due to the emerging Sino-Soviet split, Mongolia remained on observer status.
